rationale: C10 plausibly supplied a material template for the later letter’s central argument: a lengthy, fact-driven appeal about the steel industry that evaluates profits, wages and costs, rejects a steel price increase as unjustified, connects steel pricing to broader inflation, and invokes the national interest. C23 reinforces the same steel-specific logic—profits exceeding increased wage costs and any price increase requiring factual justification—but is narrower and embedded in a resignation letter. C11 parallels the broader price-stability appeal and the responsibility of business and labor, but lacks the child’s steel-specific factual structure.

shared_material.child_excerpt: The steel industry, in short, can look forward to good profits without an increase in prices.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: So you see that whether you take profits before or after taxes, the conclusion is still the same. We will never be able to prevent profiteering in this emergency if we give the steel industry special treatment and immunity from the price control rules.
shared_material.explanation: Both make steel-industry profitability the factual basis for rejecting a price increase.

shared_material.child_excerpt: A steel price increase in the months ahead could shatter the price stability which the country has now enjoyed for some time.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: And if we let prices--and wages--go up to compensate for bigger income taxes, we would obviously not be preventing inflation, we would be encouraging it.
shared_material.explanation: Both frame a steel price increase as part of a wider inflationary process rather than an isolated industry decision.

shared_material.child_excerpt: The Council of Economic Advisers has supplied me with estimates of steel industry profits after October 1, calculated on an assumption that prices are not increased.
shared_material.parent_excerpt: The Iron and Steel Institute has reported that its members--some 90% of the industry--averaged 494 million dollars in profits after taxes for the three years before Korea.
shared_material.explanation: Both letters build the presidential appeal around detailed quantitative evidence about steel profits, including after-tax profitability.

shared_material.child_excerpt: the responsible exercise of economic freedom serves the national welfare
shared_material.parent_excerpt: I want to end Government operation at the earliest possible moment, and I will do everything I can to end it as soon as that can be done without irreparable harm to the national interest.
shared_material.explanation: Both conclude the steel-pricing discussion by subordinating private industrial interests to national welfare, although the governmental circumstances differ.
